title: Given a Scenario, Troubleshoot Network Issues

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Cloud networking problems can look similar on the surface. A user may simply report that something does not work.
The real cause could involve DNS, DHCP, NTP, NAT, HTTP, latency, bandwidth, routing, VLAN configuration, or IP addressing.
The key troubleshooting skill is identifying which network function is failing from the symptom.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: What network function is supposed to happen, and what symptom identifies the broken layer or service?
sections.callout: Name resolution → DNS. Address assignment → DHCP. Time → NTP. Address translation → NAT. Web response → HTTP. Path → routing. Local segmentation → VLAN.

sections.title: Network Service Unavailability
paragraphs: A network service can fail even while the underlying network remains partially functional. CompTIA highlights DHCP, DNS, NTP, NAT, and HTTP.

sections.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP)
paragraphs: DHCP automatically provides IP configuration to devices, including an IP address, subnet information, default gateway, and DNS settings.
Think: DHCP gives the device its network identity.
sections.callout: A device cannot obtain IP configuration automatically → DHCP.

sections.title: Domain Name System (DNS)
paragraphs: DNS translates names into IP addresses.
Think: Name → address.
sections.callout: Users can reach a service by IP address but not by hostname → DNS.

sections.title: Network Time Protocol (NTP)
paragraphs: NTP synchronizes system clocks. Correct time matters for logs, authentication, certificates, and event correlation.
Think: Keep everybody's clock together.
sections.callout: Cloud systems have incorrect or inconsistent time → NTP.

sections.title: Network Address Translation (NAT)
paragraphs: NAT translates one IP addressing context into another. It is often used when private resources need connectivity through translated addresses.
Think: Translate the address before traffic leaves.
sections.callout: Private-addressed systems cannot reach destinations through the expected translated connection → NAT.

sections.title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Status Codes
paragraphs: HTTP is used for web communication, and status codes indicate what happened to a web request.
Think: The first digit identifies the result family.
sections.callout: A 404-style issue points to the client or request side. A 500-style issue points to the server side.

sections.title: Latency
paragraphs: Latency is delay. High latency means traffic takes too long to reach its destination or return.
Symptoms include slow response, delay, and lag.
Think: The connection works—it is just taking too long.
sections.callout: The main symptom is delay rather than failure → latency.

sections.title: Bandwidth/Throughput Issues
paragraphs: Bandwidth describes available network capacity. Throughput describes the amount of data actually transferred successfully over time.
A connection may exist but perform poorly because insufficient capacity is available.
Think: The road is open, but not enough traffic can move through it.
sections.callout: Large transfers are slow because not enough data can move at once → bandwidth or throughput issue.

sections.title: Network Device Misconfiguration
paragraphs: Virtual and physical networking devices depend on correct interfaces, policies, routes, gateways, and switching settings.
Think: The network is there, but somebody configured it incorrectly.
sections.callout: Connectivity broke after a network configuration change → network device misconfiguration.

entries.title: Protocol Incompatibility
paragraphs: A protocol incompatibility occurs when communicating systems do not support compatible protocols or versions.
Think: They are speaking different languages.
entries.recognitionCue: Two systems cannot communicate because their supported protocols do not match → protocol incompatibility.

entries.title: Protocol Deprecations
paragraphs: A provider may stop supporting an old protocol or protocol version. A system relying on it may stop working after support is removed.
Think: That language is no longer accepted.
entries.recognitionCue: Connectivity worked until an old protocol was retired → protocol deprecation.

entries.title: Scope Exhaustion
paragraphs: A DHCP or address pool contains a limited number of addresses. Scope exhaustion occurs when all available addresses have been assigned and new systems cannot receive one.
Think: No IP addresses are left in the bucket.
entries.recognitionCue: New systems cannot obtain addresses because the pool is full → scope exhaustion.

entries.title: Network Overlap
paragraphs: Network overlap occurs when connected networks use conflicting address ranges.
Routing becomes ambiguous because the same addresses appear in multiple places.
Think: Two neighborhoods have the same street addresses.
entries.recognitionCue: Connected networks use overlapping IP ranges → network overlap.

sections.title: Routing Issues
paragraphs: Routing determines how packets travel between different networks.

entries.title: Missing Routes
paragraphs: A missing route means the router or route table has no path for the destination. Think: No directions exist.
entries.recognitionCue: The destination network is unreachable because no route exists → missing route.

entries.title: Misconfigured Routes
paragraphs: A route may exist but point traffic in the wrong direction. Think: Directions exist—they are just wrong.
entries.recognitionCue: Traffic is sent toward the wrong gateway or path → misconfigured route.

sections.callout: Missing route → no path. Misconfigured route → wrong path.

sections.title: Switching Issues
paragraphs: Cloud and virtual networks still rely on logical switching behavior. CompTIA focuses on VLAN issues and port configuration.

entries.title: VLAN Issues
paragraphs: A VLAN logically separates network traffic. Incorrect VLAN configuration can isolate systems that should communicate or place traffic in the wrong network.
Think: The device is in the wrong logical neighborhood.
entries.recognitionCue: Devices are incorrectly separated or joined because of VLAN configuration → VLAN issue.

entries.title: Misconfigured VLAN Tags
paragraphs: A VLAN tag identifies which VLAN traffic belongs to. An incorrect tag can associate traffic with the wrong VLAN or cause it to be discarded.
Think: Wrong label on the packet.
entries.recognitionCue: Tagged traffic is assigned to the wrong logical network → misconfigured tags.

entries.title: Access vs. Trunk Ports
paragraphs: An access port normally carries traffic for one VLAN to an endpoint. A trunk port carries traffic for multiple VLANs, using tags to identify the traffic.
Think: Access = one VLAN. Trunk = many VLANs on one link.
entries.recognitionCue: One endpoint VLAN → access port. Multiple VLANs across one connection → trunk port.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: A network service fails while some connectivity remains → Network service unavailability
A device cannot obtain an IP address automatically → DHCP
IP works but hostname does not → DNS
Systems have incorrect time → NTP
Private systems cannot translate addresses → NAT
A web response contains an error number → HTTP status code
The connection works but feels delayed → Latency
Data transfers too slowly → Bandwidth/throughput
The network broke after a configuration change → Network device misconfiguration
Systems use incompatible protocols → Protocol incompatibility
An old protocol is no longer supported → Protocol deprecation
An address pool is empty → Scope exhaustion
The same subnet exists in two connected networks → Network overlap
No path exists → Missing route
The wrong path is configured → Misconfigured route
Logical network membership is wrong → VLAN issue
The VLAN identifier is wrong → Misconfigured tag
One VLAN per endpoint port → Access port
Multiple VLANs on one link → Trunk port

entries.title: DNS vs. General Connectivity
paragraphs: Do not automatically blame DNS when users cannot reach anything. If a destination works by IP address but not by hostname, DNS becomes the strong clue.

entries.title: Latency vs. Throughput
paragraphs: Latency measures delay. Throughput measures the amount of data transferred. A tiny request can suffer high latency; a giant transfer can suffer low throughput.

entries.title: Scope Exhaustion vs. DNS
paragraphs: If a device never receives a valid IP address, suspect DHCP or addressing. If it has an IP but names fail, suspect DNS.

entries.title: Missing vs. Misconfigured Route
paragraphs: No route means missing. A route that sends traffic incorrectly is misconfigured.

entries.title: Access vs. Trunk
paragraphs: Access carries one VLAN. Trunk carries multiple VLANs. If multiple VLANs need to cross a link, an access port is the wrong choice.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: No automatic IP assignment → DHCP
IP works, hostname fails → DNS
Clock synchronization fails → NTP
Private address translation fails → NAT
Web returns 4xx or 5xx → HTTP status code
Long delay → Latency
Not enough data is moving → Bandwidth or throughput
Incorrect device settings → Network device misconfiguration
Protocol versions cannot communicate → Protocol incompatibility
Old protocol removed → Protocol deprecation
No addresses left → Scope exhaustion
Two networks use the same range → Network overlap
No destination path → Missing route
Traffic follows the wrong path → Misconfigured route
Wrong logical LAN → VLAN issue
Wrong VLAN ID → Misconfigured tag
Single VLAN → Access port
Multiple VLANs → Trunk port
2xx → Success
3xx → Redirect
4xx → Client or request issue
5xx → Server issue
